result.question: Research how the best AI and tech products design their onboarding / "getting started" / installation guides. I need concrete, specific examples — not generic UX theory. Products to investigate: Anthropic/Claude, OpenAI, Linear, Vercel, Stripe, Notion, Superhuman, Raycast, Arc Browser, Perplexity AI, Cursor, Replit, Loom. For each: heading hierarchy, step-by-step guidance, tone/copy, celebration moments, and how they simplify technical concepts for non-technical users. Context: evaluating for a Hebrew-language installation guide for non-technical users setting up a personal AI agent (NanoClaw) in 8 steps.
result.summary: Cover the question from four complementary angles: (1) direct teardowns of specific products' onboarding docs and flows, (2) practitioner/designer analysis of what makes developer-tool onboarding work for non-technical users, (3) copy and tone patterns in top SaaS/AI onboarding, and (4) mobile-first and internationalization considerations for guided installation flows. A fifth angle targets the specific "scary technical step" problem — credit cards, servers, API keys — and how products de-risk those moments.

angles.rationale: Specifically targets the hardest moments in NanoClaw's flow (cloud server, credit card, API key) and how other products handle fear, trust, and cognitive load at those exact steps.

results.title: Vercel — Engineer the Empty State Out (Selection, Not Creation)
results.snippet: Vercel's onboarding never shows a blank canvas. It surfaces the user's existing Git repos so the first action is 'pick one,' not 'create something.' Framework detection auto-fills settings; the live URL is the celebration moment. Cognitive load is slashed because the system adapts to the user. NanoClaw apply: at the cloud server setup step, auto-select the simplest/cheapest option and present it as 'we recommend this — just confirm,' rather than asking the user to choose from a list of server types they cannot understand.

results.title: Superhuman — Micro-Tasks + Acknowledge Fear Before Scary Actions
results.snippet: Superhuman broke onboarding into tiny achievable micro-tasks (one shortcut, one email) and explicitly named user anxieties before asking for scary actions ('This looks complicated, but takes 90 seconds'). This doubled activation rates. Naming the fear reduces drop-off more than simplifying the UI. NanoClaw apply: each of the 8 steps should have exactly one action; and before the 'add credit card' step, add a single sentence: 'This feels scary — you won’t be charged until you choose a paid plan, and we walk you through the free tier.'

results.title: Linear — Learning Through Doing, Not Reading (Contextual Helpers, Intelligent Defaults)
results.snippet: Linear's 10+ step onboarding doesn't feel long because users learn by doing rather than reading instructions. Contextual helpers appear only when needed; intelligent defaults pre-fill fields so the first action is confirmation, not configuration. Tone: two parts instruction, one part warmth. NanoClaw apply: instead of explaining what an API key is before asking for it, show the exact input field with a highlighted screenshot of where to find the key on the provider site — instruction is embedded in the action, not before it.

results.title: Ghost & Sked Social — Progress Bars + Celebration Moments = 3–10× Activation Lift
results.snippet: Ghost found users who completed a 5-step progress bar were 1,000% more likely to convert; Sked Social's 4-step checklist with a celebration message made users 3× more likely to convert. Confetti or a clear 'Done!' state after each step provides evidence the user is succeeding and sustains momentum through intimidating sequences (the Zeigarnik effect). NanoClaw apply: add a persistent '3 of 8 steps complete' bar at the top of every step, and display a short congratulations screen after each step — especially after the two scariest ones (server setup, credit card).

results.title: Superhuman Onboarding Playbook (First Round Capital) — White-Glove Structure & Copy Principles
results.snippet: Detailed breakdown of Superhuman's full onboarding philosophy: personalized 1-on-1 coaching, six-step live session structure, and the principle that motivation peaks right after sign-up so that is when the most important prompts must land. Their team measured that each onboarding interaction must feel like an achievable micro-task, never a configuration ritual. NanoClaw apply: the guide's first screen (after the role picker) should be the highest-energy moment — not a table of contents but an immediate single action with a clear payoff ('In 20 minutes you’ll have your own AI agent. Let’s start.').

results.title: PageFlows — Linear, Vercel & Raycast Onboarding Screen-by-Screen Reference
results.snippet: PageFlows documents exact screen-by-screen onboarding flows for Linear, Vercel, and Raycast with annotated recordings — a concrete visual benchmark for heading hierarchy, button copy, step count, and transition design in top-tier products. Useful for auditing whether NanoClaw’s guide heading sizes, button labels, and step transitions match the visual language non-technical users already associate with trustworthy modern products. Progressive disclosure — showing only the current step on mobile, collapsing previous ones — is the strongest shared pattern across all three.

results.title: How Notion Crafts a Personalized Onboarding Experience: 6 Lessons to Guide New Users
results.snippet: Notion opens with a persona quiz and dynamically adapts the starting workspace based on the answer, using progressive disclosure to introduce complexity only as needed. This directly mirrors the NanoClaw challenge: different roles (sales, HR, marketing) have different fears. Apply at NanoClaw: add a one-question picker at guide entry that reframes each scary step (e.g. 'cloud server' into 'your personal storage space') in the user's own language based on their role.

results.title: Using a Progress Bar (UI) in SaaS: 5 Types + Examples — Userpilot
results.snippet: Research shows pre-filling the first progress increment lifts checklist completion by 21%. Asana uses animated creatures at completion; Loom uses a steps-remaining count with checkmarks; Grammarly labels each step in a visual bar. The key: show momentum immediately and celebrate at each step. Apply at NanoClaw: add a sticky top bar with fill animation and a micro-celebration (checkmark pop) at each step completion, especially after the intimidating server and API-key steps.

results.title: 26 Best User Onboarding Examples by Tactic (2026) — Appcues
results.snippet: Canva drops the user into a pre-filled template the moment they pick a use case — zero blank-page anxiety. Calendly shows a ready-made outcome within seconds so users understand what they get before setup. Shared pattern: show the end-state first, then walk backwards through setup. Apply at NanoClaw: open the guide with a 'what you'll have when you're done' screen showing a mock chat with the agent responding, before the user sees the server-setup step.

results.title: I studied the UX/UI of over 200 onboarding flows — here's everything I learned
results.snippet: Analysis of 200+ onboarding flows finds highest drop-off always happens at the first 'scary' action — payment info, software install, permissions. Top products neutralize this with a 'why we need this' tooltip directly beside the scary field, social proof, and a reversibility promise. Apply at NanoClaw: add a reassurance block directly above the credit-card and server-setup steps — not a separate FAQ page, but inline, at the exact moment of anxiety.

results.title: Raycast Onboarding Flow on Web — Page Flows
results.snippet: Raycast precedes every permission or system-level step with a plain-language explanation of exactly what will happen and why — no jargon. The 'Replace Spotlight' step (which overwrites a system setting) is framed as a benefit, not a warning. Apply at NanoClaw: reframe every technical step title from what-it-is to what-it-does-for-you — e.g. 'Create a cloud server' becomes 'Set up your agent's home' — and add a one-line plain-language 'why' before each action.

results.title: PLG Onboarding: Slack, Notion & Canva Success — Venue
results.snippet: Slack's onboarding is built around one 'aha moment' goal: send your first message within 2 minutes. Every design decision before that moment is ruthlessly cut. Apply at NanoClaw: define the guide's single activation moment (first message received from the agent in the user's chat app) and count steps backward from it — any step that doesn't directly unlock that moment is a candidate to defer, simplify, or reframe.

results.title: Vercel's AI-Native Customer Onboarding: How They Activate Developer Teams
results.snippet: Vercel engineers out the empty state entirely: the first screen shows the user's actual GitHub repos, so the first action is selection not creation. Framework is auto-detected, build commands are auto-filled, and a real-time streaming progress log plays during the build. The deploy finishes with a live URL and confetti as the celebration moment. Apply at NanoClaw: replace blank setup screens with pre-filled defaults and auto-detection wherever possible; end each major step with a visible 'you did it' celebration signal.

results.title: The onboarding Linear built without any AB Testing — Growth Dives
results.snippet: Linear's onboarding is 10+ steps but feels lightweight because every step is hands-on action (not reading). Optional steps (GitHub sync, invite teammates) can be skipped without blocking progress. Apply at NanoClaw: make every wizard step an action the user takes, not a page they read; mark truly optional steps clearly so non-technical users don't feel blocked by choices that don't apply to them.

results.title: SaaS Onboarding UX Examples: Patterns That Get Users to First Value | SaaSUI Blog
results.snippet: Consolidates concrete implementation patterns across top SaaS products: progress bar as a commitment device (3-5 items tied to activation milestones, not infinite steps), empty states as teaching surfaces, and progressive disclosure (reveal complexity only when relevant). Key insight: define one activation moment, then remove every step that doesn't lead to it. Apply at NanoClaw: the 8-step guide should map to 1-2 clear activation milestones (agent running, chat connected), making earlier steps feel like they are building toward something.

results.title: Superhuman's Onboarding Playbook — First Round Review
results.snippet: Superhuman built a synthetic sandbox inbox so users could practice with no real-world consequences before touching their real email, producing a 67% increase in feature usage and 17% higher activation in week 1. Apply at NanoClaw: for the scariest steps (credit card, server setup), add an explicit 'nothing bad can happen here' reassurance message and, where possible, a test/sandbox mode before the real action is taken.

results.title: Banking Onboarding: Best UX Practices from Revolut, Nubank, Monzo
results.snippet: Fintech products handle the scariest UX in consumer software and have developed specific fear-reduction patterns. Revolut breaks a daunting process into micro-steps with a progress bar; Monzo uses conversational language ('We'll need a quick selfie to keep your account secure'); Chime attaches a plain-language reason to every sensitive request ('We ask this to protect your account'). Apply at NanoClaw: for the credit card and server-creation steps, add a friendly one-sentence explanation of why this is needed and break the action into the smallest possible sub-steps with a visible progress indicator.

results.title: Notion's clever onboarding and inspirational templates — AppCues / GoodUX
results.snippet: Notion solves blank-canvas paralysis by populating the first screen with a personalized template selection (5 options based on signup answers) and a Getting Started page that teaches features by having users interact with pre-built content. Demo data makes value concrete before the user has done real work. Apply at NanoClaw: offer role-based entry points (e.g., 'I want to connect WhatsApp' vs. 'I want to connect Gmail') so the guide path feels personally relevant from step 1, reducing decision anxiety for non-technical users.

results.title: How Stripe Built a Writing Culture — Slab / Knock Down Silos
results.snippet: Stripe treats documentation as a product: a feature is not shipped until its docs are written and reviewed. Their style is brand-neutral, plain-English, audience-aware (no jargon), and structured with short paragraphs, subheads, and bullets. CEO Patrick Collison's emails include footnotes — writing is a cultural signal, not just a task. Directly applicable: NanoClaw's guide should treat every step as a 'shipped feature' — copy finalized before the step goes live, not after.

results.title: How Stripe creates the best documentation in the industry — Mintlify
results.snippet: Deep analysis of why Stripe docs are the industry benchmark: consistent imperative verbs, zero marketing-speak inside the guide, reader-centric framing ('you can now...' not 'our system will...'), progressive disclosure (show only what the user needs at this step), and live interactive examples. Directly applicable: NanoClaw's scary steps (credit card, server setup) should use Stripe's pattern of neutral framing + immediate payoff — show the user what happens right after the scary action.

results.title: Superhuman's Onboarding Playbook — First Round Review
results.snippet: Superhuman built its onboarding around one insight: users need to feel expert, not novice. Their 1-on-1 onboarding call uses language of the customer's own habits, not product jargon. Each email in their 30-day post-onboarding series is 'a masterclass in a single feature' — digestible, encouraging, one-concept-at-a-time. Directly applicable: NanoClaw's 8-step guide should give each step a single clear 'win' framing — not 'configure your VPS' but 'pick your server home in 60 seconds'.

results.title: Super informative, super fun: inside Superhuman's writing culture — Slab
results.snippet: Superhuman's internal writing mantra: 'super informative, super fun.' Every customer-facing string is tested for whether it can be shorter AND warmer simultaneously. They bank resonant phrases from actual customer language and reuse them across touchpoints. Directly applicable to NanoClaw's Hebrew copy problem: collect the actual words non-technical Hebrew users use to describe 'server' or 'API key' and mirror that language back at them in the guide.

results.title: Onboarding UX Writing — 10 microcopy examples from top onboarding flows — UserOnBoarding Academy
results.snippet: Concrete teardowns of 10 real onboarding flows focusing exclusively on microcopy: button labels, empty states, progress indicators, error messages, and celebration moments. Key pattern: top products use action verbs that describe the user's outcome ('Start recording' not 'Begin'), reassurance copy below scary fields ('We never share this', 'You can change this later'), and celebration that names the specific thing accomplished. Directly applicable: NanoClaw's CTA buttons and step completion states need this audit.

results.title: SaaS Onboarding Examples: Lessons from 20+ Top Products — Appcues
results.snippet: Survey of onboarding patterns across 20+ products including Notion, Loom, and Linear. Notion's onboarding checklist doubles as a product demo — each completed step teaches a core action rather than just checking a box. Loom strips the flow to the single action that creates the 'aha moment' and removes everything else. Key takeaway for NanoClaw: the guide's 8 steps likely contain several that are really sub-steps — collapsing or hiding them behind a 'done for you' default would reduce the intimidation factor for non-technical users.

results.title: How Stripe Uses 4 Developer-First UX Principles to Drive Massive Adoption (Raw.Studio)
results.snippet: Stripe structures every interface around a single question: 'What is the absolute minimum information needed at this step?' Their docs are task-oriented (not company-organized), with inline interactive playgrounds so users can try API calls before committing. Errors are written for non-technical readers, not engineers. Every product has a Quickstart on the left nav. Apply at NanoClaw: reframe each scary step (credit card, API key) around the minimum required action, and add a contextual 'why do I need this?' tooltip directly adjacent to the ask.

results.title: Superhuman's Onboarding Playbook (First Round Review)
results.snippet: Superhuman replaced self-serve setup with mandatory 1-on-1 concierge calls modeled on the Apple Genius Bar and 5-star hotel check-in. A human specialist walks each user through every scary step live, reducing anxiety through empathy and real-time help. Result: 65% full migration completion live on call, doubled activation rates, $650K+ ARR per specialist. Apply at NanoClaw: even a recorded walkthrough video or a live 'stuck? message us' escape hatch at the hardest steps (Render setup, credit card) borrows this principle — the user needs to feel someone is with them.

results.title: Developer Onboarding: Stripe — Cristiano Betta (DX Review)
results.snippet: Detailed teardown showing how Stripe's interactive tutorial lets users make a real API call in under 5 minutes, without signing up first. The playground shows the number of API calls, flow structure, and hidden features — learning by doing, not reading. Documentation is structured as a progressive journey from zero to first success. Apply at NanoClaw: place a 'see what this step does' preview or short screencast before users must input credentials or a credit card — reduce the unknown before the commitment.

results.title: Duolingo's Delightful User Onboarding — GoodUX / Appcues
results.snippet: Duolingo uses animated progress bars, celebratory moments after each lesson (characters reacting, streak counters, milestone badges), and micro-rewards for completing a step in a row. The onboarding never shows the full complexity upfront — it progressively reveals difficulty only once the user has built confidence through small wins. Apply at NanoClaw: after each guide step completion ('You set up your server! ✓'), add a brief celebratory message and a clear count ('Step 3 of 8 — you're 37% there') to transform fear into momentum.

results.title: Fintech Onboarding: 6 UX Practices That Reduce Drop-Off (Eleken)
results.snippet: Covers the specific moment of credit card / financial data requests in onboarding: 'No credit card required' and 'Cancel anytime' language at the point of ask dramatically reduces drop-off. Progressive verification — collect the minimum at first, delay sensitive asks until the user has experienced value — is highlighted as the key lever. Trust signals (security badges, plain-language explanations of why data is needed) placed directly adjacent to scary fields. Apply at NanoClaw: add a single reassurance line next to each sensitive step, e.g., 'This card is for Render's free server — you won't be charged unless you upgrade.'

results.title: How to Design an Effective SaaS Onboarding UX (Lollypop Design, 2025)
results.snippet: Synthesizes current best practices: onboarding checklists as progress anchors (users can see exactly what's done and what's left), animated completion badges, step-numbering that shows 'Step X of Y' prominently, and progressive disclosure that hides advanced options until the user has passed the basics. Specifically notes that information overload at technical steps is the #1 drop-off cause. Apply at NanoClaw: restructure the 8-step guide so each step shows only what's needed for that step — hide all subsequent complexity behind a 'Next' barrier, and surface a persistent step counter on mobile.

result.evidence:
The claim is refuted on three grounds:

1. METHODOLOGICAL FLAW / MISREAD OF QUOTE: The 30%→98% comparison is not an apples-to-apples measurement. The 30% baseline came from users voluntarily completing an optional checklist. The 98% figure came from a mandatory full-screen flow that users could not skip — the article explicitly states Superhuman "made onboarding steps impossible to skip." Comparing voluntary completion of an optional flow to completion of a mandatory forced flow and framing it as a 68-point improvement conflates two entirely different measurements. Near-100% completion of a forced mandatory flow is arithmetically expected, not a meaningful finding about panel design effectiveness.

2. OVERREACH ON "CHECKLISTS = ZERO IMPACT": The source says Superhuman's specific optional side-quest checklist showed "no change in activation rates." The claim under review distorts this into a general finding that checklists yield "zero impact on activation." The source makes no such general claim, and independent industry benchmarks (Userpilot 2024/2025 data) show checklists with 3–4 essential tasks increase completion 20–30% and improve 7-day retention 40–60% — contradicting the absolutist framing.

3. SOURCE QUALITY INSUFFICIENT FOR CLAIM STRENGTH: The source is a first-person narrative authored by Superhuman's own VP of Growth and published on First Round Capital's content marketing platform (a VC firm that invested in Superhuman). It provides zero methodology detail: no sample size, no time period, no definition of "completion," no control group, and no independent verification. The WebFetch of the original article confirmed: "No mention of sample size / No specified time period / No explicit definition of what constituted 'completion' / No indication this was a controlled experiment." A claim presented as a strong causal benchmark ("increased from 30% to 98%") requires far stronger evidentiary standards than a single company's unverified internal anecdote.

result.evidence:
The claim conflates two distinct Superhuman features and misattributes the 57% statistic. 

(1) The synthetic inbox was a shortcut-training sandbox: users practiced keyboard shortcuts (E to archive, R to reply, J/K to navigate) on pre-filled fake emails — its purpose was building muscle memory for shortcuts, NOT specifically "reaching Inbox Zero." Multiple sources confirm this ("no real emails, no real consequences," "drill muscle memory").

(2) "Get Me To Zero" is a separate feature that archives users' REAL old emails to clear their actual inbox — it is NOT a fake/safe environment. It does the opposite: it acts directly on live email data. The 57% opt-in stat and "close to a billion emails" belong to this real-email archiving feature, not to the synthetic inbox.

The claim fuses these two into one misleading description — "a synthetic fake inbox letting users reach Inbox Zero" — and then cites the 57% stat as if it describes usage of that fake environment. In reality, 57% of users opted in to archiving their genuine email, which directly contradicts the "no fear of touching real email" framing.

It reads as a promotional case study, not audited research.

result.summary: Only three claims survived adversarial verification across the investigated products, and they all cluster around a single coherent design philosophy: the best technical onboarding reduces perceived complexity by making defaults invisible, tone calm, and actions concrete. Linear and Slack — the two products with verified claims — both avoid overwhelming non-technical users with configuration choices upfront. Linear does this through task-based learning with minimalist, emotionally neutral copy; Slack does it by shipping a pre-configured workspace so users experience the product before they ever have to set it up. Notably, all claims about celebration mechanics, progress bars, personalization flows, sandbox environments, and first-win optimization were refuted or failed verification — suggesting those are either overstated in the UX literature or not implemented in the ways commonly described. For the NanoClaw guide, the actionable signal is narrow but high-confidence: eliminate upfront choices, make scary steps feel routine through calm copy, and have users do the thing rather than read about the thing.
